originalTitle: GCC steering committee announces AI policy
content:
The GCC steering committee has announced that it has accepted an AI contributions policy recommended by the GCC AI policy working group.

The policy, in part, states that the project will decline any " legally significant contributions which include LLM-generated content or are derived from LLM-generated content ". It uses the definition of "legally significant" from the GNU Project maintainer guidelines, which holds that the threshold is " around 15 lines of code and/or text " to qualify as significant for copyright purposes. GCC maintainers may, however, choose to accept legally significant test cases that are generated by an LLM.

The policy does not forbid use of LLMs for research, analysis, bug discovery and reporting, patch review, etc. as long as the output is not included in contributions. The committee says that it expects the policy will evolve and will be revisited periodically.

That's a naive and outdated view of how these tools work. With models at the level of Opus 4.8 or GPT 5.5 and newer in the hand of a competent programmer the result is simply indistinguishable. So much so that in systemd we simply scrapped the requirement to annotate commits with "Co-developed-by" a month ago or so, as it became completely pointless (while giving the usual shits-for-brains handy targets to abuse and harass). There are only good PRs or bad PRs, and the tools used to write them are now completely orthogonal to that. A bad PR is a bad PR, regardless of whether it is artisanal, organic, free-range and grass-fed or not. And nobody can tell the difference in good PRs. That's why these kind of rules are silly and pointless. Enough Posted Jul 30, 2026 13:54 UTC (Thu) by jzb (editor, #7867) [ Link ] (2 responses)

So given you don't have such first-hand experience, don't you feel a bit weird telling people who do have it, how their experience actually is? > That's normal bug-hunting. It's not "not understanding the code". I disagree, I would definitely qualify that as "understanding the code". Which in a way, confirms that it does happen that you don't understand your code either, but you simply don't qualify it as "understanding", which is an easy way out I guess? The generated code typically contains more information than the prompt that generated it. The source code (which may include prompts and AI instructions in md files!) is the primary and preferred form for modification, no matter if you modify it by hand or by tool (AI). legally significant Posted Jul 30, 2026 16:51 UTC (Thu) by GNUtoo (guest, #61279) [ Link ]
chineseTitle: GCC指导委员会宣布 AI 政策
chineseContent:

该政策部分规定，该项目将拒绝任何“具有法律意义的重大贡献，其中包括法学硕士生成的内容或源自法学硕士生成的内容”。它使用 GNU 项目维护者指南中“具有法律意义”的定义，该定义认为阈值是“大约 15 行代码和/或文本”，以符合版权目的。 GCC maintainers may, however, choose to accept legally significant test cases that are generated by an LLM.

该政策并不禁止使用法学硕士进行研究、分析、错误发现和报告、补丁审查等，只要输出不包含在贡献中即可。该委员会表示，预计该政策将会不断发展，并将定期重新审查。
